title: Shah Rukh Khan's Films Are at the Centre of a ₹250 Million Legal War — and NRIs Might Feel It First
excerpt: JioStar has accused Zee Entertainment of being a 'habitual infringer' for broadcasting 12 Bollywood films without authorization. The mediation hearing is May 25.
body:
The two companies that control more than half of everything Indians watch on television are now locked in a legal fight over who owns the right to broadcast some of Bollywood's biggest films — and the fallout could reshape what content reaches NRI living rooms from New York to London to Melbourne.

JioStar, the media behemoth born from the $8.5 billion merger of Reliance Industries and Disney's Indian media assets in 2024, filed a plea on May 4 before the Delhi High Court Legal Services Committee. The target: Zee Entertainment, India's second-largest broadcaster. The accusation: unauthorized broadcast of 12 Bollywood films — reportedly aired around 20 times — whose rights JioStar claims to own. Among the titles allegedly aired without permission are films starring Shah Rukh Khan and Aamir Khan, though the specific titles haven't been publicly confirmed beyond references to classics like *Deewaar* and *Dangal* in court filings.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

JioStar's 120-page plea pulls no punches. The company has branded Zee a "habitual infringer" that continues to "engage in the unauthorised broadcast and exploitation of the films." The damages being sought exceed ₹250 million (approximately $2.61 million), though the final compensation figure hasn't been locked in. The matter goes before a mediation committee on May 25, with Zee directed to appear or risk having its absence treated as a refusal to participate.

Zee's response has been carefully calibrated: the broadcasts were "inadvertent and unintentional," the company said, adding it would "exercise caution moving forward" while flatly denying liability for damages.

## A War on Multiple Fronts

This isn't an isolated skirmish. JioStar and Zee are simultaneously slugging it out in a $1 billion arbitration battle in London over the collapse of a cricket licensing agreement in 2024. And in April 2026, Zee fired back with its own lawsuit alleging JioStar had used its copyrighted music at least 50 times after licensing agreements expired — seeking $3 million in damages.

The legal artillery is flying in both directions, and the ammunition is Bollywood.

## What This Means for NRIs

Here's why this matters beyond courtroom drama. JioStar commands a 34.2 percent share of the Indian television market. Zee claims its market share has hit a four-year high of 18 percent. Together, they control over half of Indian TV.

For the diaspora, this fight is about access. When media giants dispute film rights, the casualties are often the streaming libraries and broadcast schedules that NRIs rely on. If you've ever noticed a favorite SRK classic suddenly disappearing from your streaming platform, or wondered why certain Bollywood titles aren't available internationally, this is the machinery behind it.

India's $30 billion media and entertainment market is consolidating fast. The JioStar merger created an entity with assets spanning television, streaming (JioHotstar), digital, and sports broadcasting. Zee, once courted as a merger partner itself before the deal with Sony collapsed, is now fighting to defend its turf against a rival with significantly deeper pockets.

## What's Next

The May 25 mediation hearing will be the first real test of whether these two can find middle ground — or whether this escalates into a protracted courtroom battle. Given the London arbitration already underway and the mutual lawsuits piling up, the "amicable settlement" route feels optimistic.

For NRIs watching from abroad, the practical question is simple: who controls the Bollywood library you grew up on, and what happens to your access when the people who own it can't agree on anything?

Neither company has officially commented on the latest filing.
